e-9132.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
e-9132.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/26f1037a6da42fdd87ef588234019d23d555dba8d9c02d5469215b2445da8e45.png)

The matrix above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-1,$ and $\lambda_3=3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
e-9132.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3 \times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda=-1$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda=3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block $J_1(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda=3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=-1{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block $J_2(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely $J_1(-1) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=-1.$

Computing $A+I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 7 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -9\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0} \[5pt]
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/c59f5929bdbe3b35e42dc30266ac9ca947c3536e1c019b708a2d48170ea8222b.png)

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

e-9133.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
e-9133.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/77995d8d2d70bc6eeb059663883375dbcad8820df3bafc225f854367ee122977.png)

The matrix above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda_3=2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
e-9133.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3 \times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda=2$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=2{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $3 \times 3$ Jordan block $J_3(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ corresponding to $\lambda=2$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_3 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of one $2 \times 2$ and one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block, say $J_2(2) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ corresponding to $\lambda=2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=2.$

Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2$ form the following chain: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_3 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{0}
$$

 

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/3fba5b4e0ccc48a2d122b457509e744265b2aa5cfd3625808ebb12fcd421be56.png) 

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=2, λ2=1, and λ3=−3. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

decision.explanation: The three eigenvalues 2, 1, and -3 are distinct, so A is diagonalizable. Each Jordan block has size 1, giving the diagonal Jordan canonical form diag(2,1,-3), option e. The blocks may also be reordered.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-3)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=2, λ2=1, and λ3=−3. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[20001100−3]
b
[21002000−3]
c
[21001000−3]
d
[21001100−3]
e
[20001000−3]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix that has precisely 3 distinct eigenvalues.

Therefore, A is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J1(2)⊕J1(1)⊕J1(−3)=[20001000−3].

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option e. Three distinct eigenvalues imply that A is diagonalizable, so its Jordan form consists of three size-1 blocks with diagonal entries 2, 1, and -3. Their order may vary. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-3)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

before.name: Question 2
before.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -8 \\ 2 & -2 & -4 \\ -2 & 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues 4, 2, and 0 are distinct, so A is diagonalizable. Its Jordan canonical form has three size-1 blocks, giving diag(4,2,0), option b. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -8 \\ 2 & -2 & -4 \\ -2 & 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -8 \\ 2 & -2 & -4 \\ -2 & 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues 4, 3, and 0 are distinct, so A is diagonalizable. Its Jordan canonical form consists of three size-1 blocks, giving diag(4,3,0), option a. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 \\ -2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix that has precisely 3 distinct eigenvalues.

Therefore, A is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J1(4)⊕J1(3)⊕J1(0)=[400030000].

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: distinct eigenvalues 4, 3, and 0 imply three size-1 Jordan blocks, giving diag(4,3,0). The blocks may be reordered. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 \\ -2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=8, λ2=−1, and λ3=−4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

[8000−1000−4]
Submit

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues 8, -1, and -4 are distinct, so A is diagonalizable. Its Jordan canonical form consists of three size-1 blocks, giving diag(8,-1,-4), option e. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 0 \\ -3 & -7 & 0 \\ 9 & 9 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=8,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(8)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 4

A=[260−3−70998]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=8, λ2=−1, and λ3=−4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[8100−1000−4]
b
[8100−1100−4]
c
[8000−1100−4]
d
[2100−70008]
e
[8000−1000−4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix that has precisely 3 distinct eigenvalues.

Therefore, A is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J1(8)⊕J1(−1)⊕J1(−4)=[8000−1000−4].

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 0 \\ -3 & -7 & 0 \\ 9 & 9 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=8,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(8)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues 4, 3, and -2 are distinct, so A is diagonalizable. Its Jordan canonical form has three size-1 blocks, giving diag(4,3,-2), option e. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 & 9 \\ 1 & -9 & -9 \\ -1 & 7 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

A=[7−391−9−9−177]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=4, λ2=3, and λ3=−2. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[41003000−2]
b
[3000−60005]
c
[41003100−2]
d
[3100−60005]
e
[40003000−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix that has precisely 3 distinct eigenvalues.

Therefore, A is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

J1(4)⊕J1(3)⊕J1(−2)=[40003000−2].

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 & 9 \\ 1 & -9 & -9 \\ -1 & 7 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: A-2I has rows (3,-3,-7), (-3,3,5), and (2,-2,-4). Its second column is the negative of its first, while the first two rows are independent, so its rank is 2 and nullity is 1. Thus eigenvalue 2 has one size-2 Jordan block. Eigenvalue 4 has one size-1 block, giving option b. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 5 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =2.$

Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 5 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 form the following chain: v2→A−2Iv1→A−2I0
  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(2)⊕J1(2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 form the following chains: v1→A−2I0v2→A−2I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=2.

Computing A−2I, we get

A−2I=[5−3−7−3552−2−2]−2[100010001]=[3−3−7−3352−2−4].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A−2I=[3−3−7−3352−2−4]R1↔R3∼[2−2−43−3−7−335]R2:=R2+(−32)R1R3:=R3+32R1∼[2−2−400−100−1]R3:=R3+(−1)R2∼[2−2−400−1000]

Since nullity(A−2I)=1, there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=2, say, v1. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 form the following chain:

v2→A−2Iv1→A−2I0

Therefore, we have case I, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(4)⊕J2(2)=[400021002]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 5 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =2.$

Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 5 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -7 \\ -3 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: A+2I has rows (0,0,0), (3,3,3), and (3,3,3), so its rank is 1 and nullity is 2. Thus eigenvalue -2 has two independent eigenvectors and two size-1 Jordan blocks. Together with the size-1 block for eigenvalue 4, this gives option b. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 7
?

A=[−200313331]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=−2, and λ3=4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[4100−2100−2]
b
[4000−2000−2]
c
[40004000−2]
d
[41004000−2]
e
[4000−2100−2]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix with the following eigenvalues:

  • λ=−2 of algebraic multiplicity 2

  • λ=4 of algebraic multiplicity 1

As a result, we have one 1×1 Jordan block J1(4) corresponding to λ=4. However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=−2:

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chain: v2→A+2Iv1→A+2I0

  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(−2)⊕J1(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chains: v1→A+2I0v2→A+2I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−2.

Computing A+2I, we get

A+2I=[−200313331]+2[100010001]=[000333333].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A+2I=[000333333]R1↔R2∼[333000333]R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[333000000]

Since nullity(A+2I)=2, there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue λ=−2, say, v1 and v2. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chains:

v1→A+2I0v2→A+2I0

Therefore, we have case II, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(4)⊕J1(−2)⊕J1(−2)=[4000−2000−2]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that A+2I has rank 1 and nullity 2. Therefore, eigenvalue -2 has two size-1 Jordan blocks, and eigenvalue 4 has one size-1 block. This gives diag(4,-2,-2), option b, up to block order. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 8
?

A=[−9−2−42−4242−1]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=−5, and λ3=−4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[−4000−5000−5]
b
[−4100−4000−5]
c
[−4000−4000−5]
d
[−4000−5100−5]
e
[−4100−5100−5]
Submit

decision.explanation: A+5I has rows (-4,-2,-4), (2,1,2), and (4,2,4), all multiples of (2,1,2). Thus its rank is 1 and nullity is 2, so eigenvalue -5 has two size-1 Jordan blocks. Together with the size-1 block for -4, this gives option a. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-5$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =-4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(-4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-5:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-5.$

Computing $A+5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+5I & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]+5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+5I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+5I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 8

A=[−9−2−42−4242−1]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=−5, and λ3=−4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[−4000−5000−5]
b
[−4100−4000−5]
c
[−4000−4000−5]
d
[−4000−5100−5]
e
[−4100−5100−5]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix with the following eigenvalues:

  • λ=−5 of algebraic multiplicity 2

  • λ=−4 of algebraic multiplicity 1

As a result, we have one 1×1 Jordan block J1(−4) corresponding to λ=−4. However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=−5:

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(−5). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−5 form the following chain: v2→A+5Iv1→A+5I0

  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(−5)⊕J1(−5). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−5 form the following chains: v1→A+5I0v2→A+5I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−5.

Computing A+5I, we get

A+5I=[−9−2−42−4242−1]+5[100010001]=[−4−2−4212424].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A+5I=[−4−2−4212424]R1:=−12R1∼[212212424]R2:=R2+(−1)R1R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[212000000]

Since nullity(A+5I)=2, there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue λ=−5, say, v1 and v2. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−5 form the following chains:

v1→A+5I0v2→A+5I0

Therefore, we have case II, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(−4)⊕J1(−5)⊕J1(−5)=[−4000−5000−5]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-5$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =-4$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(-4)$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-5:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-5.$

Computing $A+5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+5I & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]+5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+5I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+5I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+5I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-5)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: A+2I has rows (-6,-4,-8), (-9,4,-2), and (9,1,7). Its upper-left 2×2 minor is -60, so its rank is at least 2. Since -2 is an eigenvalue, its rank is exactly 2 and nullity is 1. Thus -2 has one size-2 Jordan block, while 3 has one size-1 block, giving option b. Block order may vary.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda =3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

A=[−8−4−8−92−2915]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=−2 and λ3=3. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[3100−2100−2]
b
[3000−2100−2]
c
[31003000−2]
d
[30003000−2]
e
[3000−2000−2]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix with the following eigenvalues:

  • λ=−2 of algebraic multiplicity 2

  • λ=3 of algebraic multiplicity 1

As a result, we have one 1×1 Jordan block J1(3) corresponding to λ=3. However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=−2:

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chain: v2→A+2Iv1→A+2I0
  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(−2)⊕J1(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chains: v1→A+2I0v2→A+2I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−2.

Computing A+2I, we get

A+2I=[−8−4−8−92−2915]+2[100010001]=[−6−4−8−94−2917].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A+2I=[−6−4−8−94−2917]R2:=R2+(−32)R1R3:=R3+32R1∼[−6−4−8010100−5−5]R3:=R3+12R2∼[−6−4−801010000]

Since nullity(A+2I)=1, there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−2, say, v1. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chain:

v2→A+2Iv1→A+2I0

Therefore, we have case I, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(3)⊕J2(−2)=[3000−2100−2]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

verification.explanation: The revealed row reduction confirms that A+2I has rank 2 and nullity 1. Hence the repeated eigenvalue -2 has one size-2 Jordan block, and eigenvalue 3 has one size-1 block, giving option b. The blocks may be reordered. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda =3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: A-3I has rows (-8,8,8), (-2,2,2), and (-4,4,4), all multiples of (-2,2,2). Its rank is 1 and nullity is 2, so eigenvalue 3 has two size-1 Jordan blocks. Together with the size-1 block for eigenvalue 1, this gives option a. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(1)$ corresponding to $\lambda =1.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =3:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =3.$

Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ -8 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=3, and λ3=1. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix with the following eigenvalues:

  • λ=3 of algebraic multiplicity 2

  • λ=1 of algebraic multiplicity 1

As a result, we have one 1×1 Jordan block J1(1) corresponding to λ=1. However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=3:

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(3). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=3 form the following chain: v2→A−3Iv1→A−3I0

  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(3)⊕J1(3). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=3 form the following chains: v1→A−3I0v2→A−3I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=3.

Computing A−3I, we get

A−3I=[−588−252−447]−3[100010001]=[−888−222−444].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A−3I=[−888−222−444]R1↔R2∼[−222−888−444]R2:=R2+(−4)R1R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[−222000000]

Since nullity(A−3I)=2, there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue λ=3, say, v1 and v2. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=3 form the following chains:

v1→A−3I0v2→A−3I0

Therefore, we have case II, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(3)⊕J1(3)⊕J1(1)=[300030001]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(1)$ corresponding to $\lambda =1.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =3:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =3.$

Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ -8 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

decision.explanation: A-5I has three identical nonzero rows (0,1,-1), so its rank is 1 and nullity is 2. Therefore there are two Jordan blocks for eigenvalue 5. Their sizes sum to 3, so they are 2 and 1, giving option c. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =5:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$

Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd  one). So, the rank of $A-5I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-5I) & =3-\text{rank}(A-5I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A-5I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 11
?

A=[51−106−1014]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=λ3=5. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[500050005]
b
[−5100−5100−5]
c
[510050005]
d
[51005100−5]
e
[510051005]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a non-scalar 3×3 matrix that has the eigenvalue λ=5 of algebraic multiplicity 3.

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=5:

  • Case I. We may have the single 3×3 Jordan block J3(5). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1,v2 and v3 corresponding to λ=5 form the following chain: v3→A−5Iv2→A−5Iv1→A−5I0

  • Case II. We may have a composition of one 2×2 and one 1×1 Jordan block, say J2(5)⊕J1(5). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1,v2 and v3 corresponding to λ=5 form the following chains: v2→A−5Iv1→A−5I0v3→A−5I0

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=5.

Computing A−5I, we get

A−5I=[51−106−1014]−5[100010001]=[01−101−101−1].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A−5I=[01−101−101−1]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[01−100001−1]R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[01−1000000]

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd one). So, the rank of A−5I is 1. Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

nullity(A−5I)=3−rank(A−5I)=3−1=2.

Recall that the nullity of A−5I gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to λ=5. Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, v1 and v3. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=1 form the following chains:

v2→A−5Iv1→A−5I0v3→A−5I0

Therefore, we have case II, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J2(5)⊕J1(5)=[510050005]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms rank(A-5I)=1 and nullity(A-5I)=2. Thus there are two Jordan blocks for eigenvalue 5, of sizes 2 and 1, giving option c, up to block order. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e. The solution's mention of eigenvalue 1 is a typo; the eigenvalue is 5.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =5:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$

Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd  one). So, the rank of $A-5I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-5I) & =3-\text{rank}(A-5I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A-5I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

decision.explanation: A+4I has three identical nonzero rows (0,1,-1), so its rank is 1 and nullity is 2. Therefore, there are two Jordan blocks for eigenvalue -4. Their sizes sum to 3, so they have sizes 2 and 1, giving option e. The blocks may be reordered.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =-4$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$  

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-4:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(-4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$

Computing $A+4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, the rank of $A+4I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A+4I) & =3-\text{rank}(A+4I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A+4I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-4$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 12
?

A=[−41−10−3−101−5]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=λ3=−4. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[−4000−4000−4]
b
[−4100−4100−4]
c
[−4100−40004]
d
[410041004]
e
[−4100−4000−4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a non-scalar 3×3 matrix that has the eigenvalue λ=−4 of algebraic multiplicity 3.

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=−4:

  • Case I. We may have the single 3×3 Jordan block J3(−4). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1,v2 and v3 corresponding to λ=−4 form the following chain: v3→A+4Iv2→A+4Iv1→A+4I0

  • Case II. We may have a composition of one 2×2 and one 1×1 Jordan block, say J2(−4)⊕J1(−4). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1,v2 and v3 corresponding to λ=−4 form the following chains: v2→A+4Iv1→A+4I0v3→A+4I0

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−4.

Computing A+4I, we get

A+4I=[−41−10−3−101−5]+4[100010001]=[01−101−101−1].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A+4I=[01−101−101−1]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[01−100001−1]R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[01−1000000]

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd one). So, the rank of A+4I is 1. Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

nullity(A+4I)=3−rank(A+4I)=3−1=2.

Recall that the nullity of A+4I gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−4. Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, v1 and v3. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−4 form the following chains:

v2→A+4Iv1→A+4I0v3→A+4I0

Therefore, we have case II, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J2(−4)⊕J1(−4)=[−4100−4000−4]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =-4$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$  

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-4:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(-4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =-4$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$

Computing $A+4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, the rank of $A+4I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A+4I) & =3-\text{rank}(A+4I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A+4I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-4.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-4$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A+4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
